title_en: Letter to the Emperor Jovian on the Faith
author: Athanasius of Alexandria
occasion: The emperor Jovian asked Athanasius to explain the faith of the catholic Church. Athanasius responds by presenting the Nicene Creed and warning against those who pretend to confess the Nicene faith while in truth denying it by reinterpreting 'homoousios' and blaspheming the Holy Spirit.
argument: Athanasius commends Jovian's desire to learn the Church's faith and presents the creed confessed by the Fathers at Nicaea as the true, apostolic faith. He explains that Arius and his followers corrupted this faith by teaching that the Son is from non-being, a creature, a work, and changeable, and that some now, wishing to renew the Arian heresy, have dared to reject the faith confessed at Nicaea, and while pretending to confess it, in truth deny it by reinterpreting 'homoousios' and blaspheming the Holy Spirit by saying it is a creature and a work made through the Son. He insists that the Nicene faith is held by churches throughout the world and must not be altered. The letter closes by quoting the Nicene Creed and its anathemas, explaining why the Fathers wrote 'homoousios' rather than merely 'like' the Father, and noting that they did not alienate the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son but glorified it with them in the one faith of the holy Trinity, because there is one divinity in the holy Trinity.

outline.move: Athanasius praises Jovian's pious desire to learn, recalls the Nicene faith, and describes how Arius and later opponents corrupted it while churches everywhere hold to Nicaea.
Athanasius quotes the Nicene Creed with its anathemas, urges Jovian to hold it unchanged, and explains the meaning of 'homoousios' and the inclusion of the Holy Spirit.

cast.name: Athanasius
cast.who: Bishop of Alexandria and author of the letter.

cast.name: Jovian
cast.who: Roman emperor to whom the letter is addressed.

cast.name: Arius
cast.who: Heretic who taught that the Son of God is from non-being, a creature, a work, and changeable.

voices.speaker: Nicene Fathers (quoted creed)
voices.how_marked: Introduced as the faith confessed at Nicaea and quoted directly.

voices.speaker: Arians (quoted slogans)
voices.how_marked: Quoted as their sayings: 'there was when he was not,' 'before being begotten he was not,' 'from non-being he came to be,' or 'from another hypostasis or essence,' or saying the Son of God is 'created,' or 'changeable,' or 'alterable.'

key_terms.sense: The Son is of the same being or essence as the Father, not merely similar.
The universal Church, as opposed to heretical factions.
The teaching of Arius that the Son is from non-being, a creature, a work, and changeable.
A created thing; the Arians applied this to the Son.
Something made; the Arians applied this to the Son.
The Arian claim that the Son came into being from non-being.
Changeable; the Arians said the Son is subject to change.
In the anathema, a distinct reality or substance from which the Son might be said to come.
Being or essence; the Son is begotten from the Father's essence.
The Holy Spirit, whom some heretics called a creature made through the Son.
The Holy Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, sharing one divinity.
Followers of Arius, used as a polemical label.

scripture: The letter quotes the Nicene Creed rather than Scripture directly. Biblical allusions follow Septuagint usage; no specific LXX book names or Psalm numbering require conversion here.
uncertain: The exact date of composition within Jovian's reign (363–364) is not stated in the text.
